newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis push for new Lebanon policy after crash.
newsitem.headline: Israelis push for new Lebanon policy after crash.

text.p: A group of Israeli lawmakers and veteran security men want the government to reconsider policy in Lebanon after 73 soldiers died in a crash of two helicopters flying there, one of the legislators said on Sunday.

Former Shin Bet secret service man Gideon Ezra, now a member of parliament from the ruling Likud party, said he called the meeting of about 10 people on Saturday night to collect "new thinking" for Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai.

The crash, the worst military air disaster in Israeli history, set the stage for renewed debate over the soldiers' destination: an anti-guerrilla occupation zone which Israel carved out in south Lebanon 12 years ago.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ruled out on Friday a unilateral Israeli withdrawal from the 15 km (nine-mile)-wide "security zone," saying it would bring Iranian-financed Hizbollah "terrorists" closer to Israel's northern Galilee.

Netanyahu said Israel would have to stabilise its northern border before it could leave and that would be difficult without agreement from Syria, Israel's arch-foe and the main power broker in Lebanon.

Netanyahu said he would have pulled Israeli troops out of Lebanon if he believed there was a "high probability" that fighters from Hizbollah -- the Party of God -- would not deploy in the vacated areas.
Ezra's group included parliament members from four political parties, former generals and other former Shin Bet men.
"We wanted to raise various ideas about the continuation of the process in Lebanon," Ezra told Israel Radio.
"We are speaking of things that must be done from tomorrow morning," he told army radio in another interview.
None of the participants would go into specifics about the proposals. Ezra said they wanted to speak first to Mordechai.

Another participant, former West Bank settlers leader Yisrael Harel, said he believed it was time to come up with a new military-political initiative after years of stagnation in Lebanon that had been costly to Israel.

The soldiers were flying to avoid Hizbollah roadside bombs that have claimed the lives of dozens of Israelis. Nearly 200 soldiers have died fighting guerrillas in Lebanon since Israel set up the occupation zone in mid-1985.
"Israeli army soldiers are working today in impossible conditions that don't add substantially to the peace of the Galilee in my assessment or their own personal security," Harel told army radio.
Uzi Landau, the hardline Likud party chairman of parliament's foreign affairs and defence committee, said both Syria and Lebanon should pay for the heavy damage inflicted by Hizbollah on Israel.

"There are two addresses in Lebanon -- one is the Lebanese government and the second address is Syria, beyond Hizbollah. Their economic and military interests must be hit," said Landau, who is not a member of Netanyahu's inner circle.
